articles.summary: Escalating nuclear threats and a Brexit rethink  Euronews.comPutin warns West that Russia is ready to use every weapon to protect Kaliningrad  BBCPutin warns West that Russia is prepared to use ‘all weapons’ to protect Kaliningrad  CNNRussia sends nuclear warning to NATO as tensions rise in the Baltic  ReutersPutin says ‘all weapons at disposal’ if there’s an attack on Russia – as it happened  The Guardian
articles.full_text:
Good morning, I’m Mared Gwyn. Welcome to your Thursday newsletter. Today: NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte tells Euronews that Russia should stop issuing nuclear threats, and the UK Prime Minister puts EU membership back on the table.
Nuclear tensions: In an interview with Euronews, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte has told Russia to stop issuing nuclear threats, after Moscow sent a letter to the alliance saying it is prepared to deploy its nuclear arsenal if its territory – including the enclave of Kaliningrad – comes under attack.
‘Stop’: "We are a defensive alliance. Stop the nuclear threats. This is absolutely not called for and not helpful," Rutte exclusively told the Euronews Defence and Space Summit on Wednesday, at a moment of heightened tension between Russia and the West.
Rutte, however, dismissed the immediate threat to the alliance’s members, saying "we will defend every inch of NATO territory”.
“That threat is not there, and if anything happens, we are ready to counter it,” he explained.
Reuters first reported that Russia had warned NATO in a document that it could resort to nuclear weapons if the alliance attempted to annex the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad, while also threatening strikes on “decision-making centres” in NATO member states from the outset of a conflict.
‘Worst-case scenario’: Earlier on Wednesday, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev – also speaking at Euronews’ summit – called for European dialogue with Russia to avert a nuclear attack. While rejecting the Kremlin’s escalatory rhetoric, Radev reminded his European counterparts of the “nuclear card”, noting Russia would be prone to play it if weakened or cornered.
"We cannot close our eyes (to the fact) that there are nuclear weapons on our continent, there are nuclear weapons in the arsenal of Russia. And this is part of the game calculation,” Radev said.
Making Putin feel that ‘war is coming’: The European Commissioner for Defence, Andrius Kubilius, rejectedRadev’s call for diplomatic engagement, warning it could embolden President Putin and undermine Ukraine.
"Russians are standing with their position very clear: Ukraine needs to surrender - that is their diplomacy position," Kubilius told Euronews, adding that Putin needs to “feel that war is coming to Russia itself”.
‘Made in Europe’ under fire: A push from Brussels to prioritise domestic European companies in defence contracts was also front and centre of the debate on Wednesday. NATO chief Rutte described the debate as a “luxury”, warning that the initiative ignores a basic problem: Europe's defence industry cannot produce enough.
Earlier on Wednesday, the US Ambassador to the EU, Andrew Puzder, slammed the EU’s “Buy European” weapons push as “self-interest”, saying it could disrupt the transatlantic defence industrial base and benefit Europe’s "enemies".
"One attack by a powerful adversary on a member state, and we’ll all be glad that we focused on weapon superiority rather than regional economics," Puzder told the summit audience.
My colleagues and I have more takeaways from the summit for you inthis debrief.
Migration talks: Home Affairs Ministers are meeting in Luxembourg with migration top of the agenda. Ministers are expected to discuss proposed measures to tackle irregular arrivals under the European Emergency Response Framework, expected to be unveiled by the Commission next month.
EU sources tell my colleague Vincenzo Genovese that the proposal is expected to include a temporary suspension of asylum rights.
Italy extends border controls: The meeting comes as tensions between Italy and Spain escalate again, after Rome extended aerial and maritime border checks with Spain by another 15 days in response to the situation in the enclave of Ceuta, where 80,000 migrants entered in an unprecedented mass entry in July.
Meanwhile, a delegation of MEPs visited the Spanish exclave on Wednesday, denouncing the attacks and smear campaigns directed against activists and organisations working on the ground by far-right groups.
French and Spanish leaders welcome Andy Burnham’s suggestion UK could go ‘all the way’ and rejoin the EU
French President Emmanuel Macron and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez have welcomed Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s suggestion that the UK could look to rejoin the EU, with Macron saying “welcome back” when asked about the prospect during a press conference in Madrid.
“If the British want to come back and if the Prime Minister is moving in that direction, I think that is very good news, both for his country and for the Europeans,” Macron said, speaking alongside Spain’s Pedro Sánchez, who also said the UK would be welcome back in the bloc.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Wednesday floated going “all the way” and rejoining the EU, as he vowed to scope out options for future EU-UK ties.
“We could stay as we are. We could look at what George Osborne has said about a customs union, we could look at what the Liberal Democrats said about the (EU) single market, or we could go all the way," Burnham said.
The UK leader also said that the EU-UK summit postponed in July amid Starmer’s resignation would be held in November.
Burnham has so far been perceived as much less focused on international and EU affairs than his predecessor Keir Starmer, leaving EU officials second-guessing his intentions for resetting relations with the bloc. But his statements now offer the clearest indication yet that his government is prepared to consider a much more ambitious overhaul of post-Brexit ties with Brussels. More.
More from our newsrooms
Methane is responsible for 30% of global warming – so why is the EU trying to delay rules to cut it? The EU has proposed to delay new rules to cut planet-warming emissions from methane, saying a delay would “relax” pressure on energy markets and therefore cut oil and gas prices. But will the new regulation really push up oil and gas prices, and how harmful are methane emissions? Ruth Wright explains.
Hundreds held, dozens wounded as protests over conditions in French schools escalate. French security forces detained more than 600 people while dozens of police and gendarmes were wounded as protests that have seen blockades of high schools and violent clashes escalated, the interior minister said on Wednesday. Christina Molle and Gavin Blackburn havethe details.

Flydubai flight FZ1073 to Israel made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia as passengers describe harrowing scenes of a fight between the pilots, with one of them stabbed. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said a pilot "attempted to crash the plane," as Israeli security services investigate.More.
We're also keeping an eye on
- European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen continues her Western Balkan tour in Kosovo and Montenegro.
- European Commissioner for the Economy Valdis Dombrovskis visits Chișinău, Moldova, and delivers a keynote speech at the National Bank of Moldova’s annual conference.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has ruled out a ceasefire on long-range strikes with Ukraine as Moscow steps up its campaign of aerial attacks on Kyiv.
“We are told: ‘Let them stop striking your refineries, and you will stop striking their ships.’ It is simply ridiculous,” Putin said on Thursday at the Valdai political forum in Moscow.

The remarks followed a meeting between United States President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in New York on September 22, when Zelenskyy said Kyiv was ready to cease strikes on Russian oil refineries and other energy facilities if Moscow also stopped its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Speaking at the forum of the Moscow-based think tank, Putin said Ukraine had “partially achieved its objectives” with these strikes, with attacks on Russian oil refineries having cost the country 1 percent of its gross domestic product (GDP), but added that Russia was now responding in kind.
Russia has ramped up long-range strikes, targeting Ukraine’s steel companies as well as supply chains, notably in the rail sector. Ukraine accuses Moscow of deliberately hitting civilian targets and keeping Kyiv on a near-constant state of alert as it braces for another tough winter.
A Russian drone struck a school in Kyiv on Thursday, according to city officials, as the Ukrainian capital endured relentless aerial attacks. No casualties were reported as children and staff at the school were in shelters when the drone hit.
Putin added that Russia would prefer to end the conflict in Ukraine through talks and wanted it to be a neutral country after the end of hostilities.
The nuclear option
He warned the West not to escalate the standoff over Ukraine by threatening the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, which is wedged between Poland and Lithuania, and pledged to defend it with nuclear weapons if necessary.
“If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation – in this case, we are referring to Kaliningrad, and perhaps other territories as well – the question of the Russian Federation deploying all the weapons at our country’s disposal will, of course, inevitably and immediately be on the agenda,” he said.
Putin’s comments followed a diplomatic note which NATO said this week it had received from Russia, warning the Western military alliance it would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if NATO attempted to cut off Russia’s Baltic exclave.
Putin warned that cycles of escalation in international conflict could quickly lead to dangerous scenarios. “We must realise that the moment when nothing can be changed any longer may come very quickly and unexpectedly for everyone. The logic of escalating, increasingly harsh retaliatory measures leads to a fatal point of no return,” he said.
On the contrary, in the event of a “favourable scenario”, Putin said the assets of Western companies that Moscow had seized could potentially be returned. Putin last month ordered the seizure of businesses and assets of Swiss food giant Nestle, French retailer Auchan, the former Leroy Merlin DIY chain and German wholesaler and food retailer Metro.

articles.title: Putin Says World Is Living Through a Dangerous Moment, Warns West Not to Escalate - The Moscow Times
articles.summary: Putin Says World Is Living Through a Dangerous Moment, Warns West Not to Escalate  The Moscow TimesRussia’s Putin rules out ceasefire with Ukraine during speech in Moscow  Al JazeeraPutin threatens to go nuclear if Russia faces crushing defeat  The TimesPutin Warns West Over Kaliningrad, Admits Ukrainian Strikes Cut Russia's GDP by 1%  UNITED24 MediaPutin claims his priority is Russia's problems, but occupied territories will also be addressed  У...

President Vladimir Putin said on Thursday the world was living through a dangerous moment and warned the West not to escalate a standoff over Ukraine by threatening the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, which Moscow has made clear it would defend with nuclear weapons if necessary.
Locked in a war in Ukraine which he said Russia had no choice but to launch in order to safeguard its own security, Putin said Russia had no plans to attack any European country and wanted to coexist peacefully.
But he reiterated that Moscow would resort to all weapons in its arsenal, including nuclear ones, if its most westerly territory — Kaliningrad, which is wedged between Poland and Lithuania — was threatened.
"If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation – in this case, we are referring to Kaliningrad, and perhaps other territories as well — the question of the Russian Federation deploying all the weapons at our country’s disposal will, of course, inevitably and immediately be on the agenda," Putin told the Valdai Forum of international Russia experts in Moscow.
"This is inevitable," he said.
Putin said Russia realized it would be facing "an enemy [NATO] twice our size."
"And we will have to make use of our competitive advantages in this struggle. Yes, of course, France and Britain are nuclear powers — we understand that perfectly well and are fully aware of it," he said. "But no one else possesses the kind of weapons that Russia has today. That is our competitive advantage."
Nuclear warning
Putin's comments followed a diplomatic note which NATO said this week it had received from Russia, warning the Western military alliance it would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if NATO attempted to cut off Russia's Baltic exclave.
Russia's warning highlighted Moscow's urgent concern at what it has presented as a growing NATO threat to Kaliningrad, a heavily militarized Russian territory that is slightly bigger than the U.S. state of Connecticut. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said the alliance had responded by emphasising that it was a defensive alliance and that nuclear threats were not helpful.
Relations, already dire since Putin's decision to send troops into Ukraine in 2022, have worsened this year, with European governments accusing Moscow of stepping up a "hybrid war" on the continent through acts including sabotage and arson.
Russia denies that, and rejects repeated statements by Western politicians that it is gearing up for a possible military attack on a NATO country.
Putin warned that cycles of escalation in international conflict could quickly lead to dangerous scenarios.
"We must realize that the moment when nothing can be changed any longer may come very quickly and unexpectedly for everyone. The logic of escalating, increasingly harsh retaliatory measures leads to a fatal point of no return," he said.
"At the heart of this escalation lie arrogance and overconfidence. This is a path to the brink of the abyss. All the more so today, when the arsenals of the world’s leading powers contain weapons capable of destroying all life or, at the very least, reducing the Earth to a catastrophic state," Putin said.
"Can we be certain that these weapons will never be used? Well, of course not. We must bear this in mind and avoid such an outcome," he added.
Putin, who said he was ready for a trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump if a proper agenda was worked out first, ruled out the idea of stopping Russian strikes on Ukrainian targets in the Black Sea area, while conceding that Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries across Russia had cost Russia 1% of its gross domestic product (GDP).
He said Russia was now responding to Ukraine in kind.
But while he cast Western help to Kyiv when it came to launching deep strikes inside Russia as a future threat, he said Moscow was not planning to attack arms factories in Europe which supplied Ukraine "tomorrow."

articles.title: The Sudan connection: Could fighting centered on Tigray draw Ethiopia into a proxy war? - DW.com
articles.summary: The Sudan connection: Could fighting centered on Tigray draw Ethiopia into a proxy war?  DW.com
articles.full_text:
Over the past week, three militias from a new alliance, led by the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), have been fighting the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) in northern Ethiopia.
The heterogeneous alliance that calls itself the "Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival" brings together seven armed domestic groups that oppose Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's federal government.
However, the ENDF has painted a picture of an alliance that extends far beyond Ethiopia's borders: Its commander-in-chief, Field Marshal Birhanu Jula, accused Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt of supporting the TPLF.
Sudan dismissed the allegation as "baseless." Its military government countered with accusations that Ethiopia was supporting the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia that has been fighting Sudan's army for over three years.
Eritrea said Ethiopia was attempting to shift responsibility for its own internal conflicts onto its neighbors. Cairo, meanwhile, issued a flat denial.
A domestic conflict with "external actors"
Viewing developments in northern Ethiopia as a domestic affair is not the full picture, according to experts.
"While it is primarily a domestic conflict, it certainly has a foreign policy dimension due to the many external actors directly or indirectly involved," said Susanne Stollreiter, the head of the Ethiopia office of the Germany's Friedrich Ebert Foundation.
Stollreiter told DW that these actors have their own interests in the region — interests that could potentially be advanced by the conflict.
"If this conflict escalates, I would even assume that it could truly lead to a kind of conflagration across the region, given the various conflict dynamics here in the Horn of Africa."
Mirroring alliances between Ethiopia and Sudan
Egypt and Sudan have long harbored grievances against Ethiopia because the source country of the Blue Nile dammed the river just before the border.
Sudan has been caught up in a brutal civil war since April 2023. Both sides to the conflict — the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the RSF militia — are believed to have ties to partners that are now fighting on opposing sides in Ethiopia.
On one hand there's the Sudanese government and the TPLF, which was largely defeated in the 2020–22 Tigray War in Ethiopia. Many Tigrayan fighters went into exile in Sudan where they organized as "Army 70" and fought alongside the SAF against the RSF.
"They played quite an important role in the Sudan Armed Forces pushing back against the RSF in eastern Sudan and even into Khartoum. And then that relationship continued," said Magnus Taylor, Deputy Project Manager, Horn of Africa at the think tank International Crisis Group (ICG).
"The issue that the federal government of Ethiopia has is that it appears that Sudan is in a kind of alignment or an alliance with one of the strongest opposition groups in the country."
Tigrayan fighters in Sudan and training camp for Sudan militia in Ethiopia
In May, the Sudanese government hosted high-ranking representatives of the TPLF and leaders of other Ethiopian groups that are critical of Abiy. Some of those groups are now part of the new seven-member alliance.
On the other hand, there's the Ethiopia's central government and the former Sudanese special unit, the RSF.
In February, the news agency Reuters reported on a secret training camp for RSF fighters in the Ethiopian border region of Benishangul-Gumuz. According to the report, the United Arab Emirates provided instructors, funding, and logistical support — claims the UAE denied.
The UAE is closely allied with Ethiopia and, despite denials, is considered the RSF's most important backer.
Is Eritrea involved in the latest conflict?
So far, there are no signs of direct involvement by the Sudanese army or the RSF in the conflict in Ethiopia. There is no evidence of Eritrea's role in the latest escalation either. But there's no shortage of wild speculation.
Eritrea fought alongside Abiy's forces in the Tigray War but the leaders of the two countries had had a falling out by the time the Pretoria peace agreement was signed in November 2022.
Experts have long suggested that Eritrea — despite denials — is now supporting the TPLF. Distrust of Abiy runs deep, given his stated ambitions to secure Ethiopia access to the open sea — by force if necessary, such as by seizing the Eritrean port of Assab on the Red Sea.
ICG analyst Magnus Taylor told DW that Eritrean involvement in the latest fighting is plausible.
"I think the Eritreans have used the TPLF and other opposition groups to deter the perceived risk of Ethiopian aggression, whether that's for access to the port or other reasons," Taylor said.
"Having a large physical presence within Tigray or within Afar even would be, I guess, a justification for the Ethiopians to carry out more extensive military operations on Eritrea. The Eritrean tactic is to deter military action, not to invite it."
Asmara has strengthened relations with Cairo this year, and the United States has just let sanctions against Eritrea expire.
Is there a risk of a wider regional conflict in the Horn of Africa?
The Horn of Africa borders the Gulf region in the north, which has lost stability due to the Iran war. Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels are also disrupting the Bab al-Mandab Strait. .
In Somalia, Al-Shabab is regaining ground, cooperating with the Houthis despite wide ideological differences.
"These are important trade routes that are being disputed and fought over and everyone is trying to profit from the unstable situation," Stollreiter, the head of the Ethiopia office of the Germany's Friedrich Ebert Foundation, said.
"In this respect, it is no real coincidence that so many actors are now becoming particularly strong again, also because of the absence of the actors who were otherwise protective powers in the region."
The US in particular, but also the Europeans tied down by Russia's war in Ukraine, have less of an eye on the Horn of Africa than before, Stollreiter said.
Have Gulf powers taken sides in Ethiopia?
The UAE and Saudi Arabia, which are accused of supporting different warring parties in Sudan and Yemen, and have polarized the entire region in recent years, are all the more present.
However, ICG's Magnus Taylor does not think that the situation in Ethiopia is at risk of escalating into a proxy war between the Gulf powers.
"While the UAE is a strong backer of Addis Ababa, the Saudis are not strongly backing the TPLF or any other opposition group."
Whether from the Arabian Peninsula, Sudan, or Eritrea — one week after the outbreak of war in Ethiopia, there are no clear signs that the internal conflict is becoming internationalized. However, in the unstable Horn of Africa, that risk is particularly high.
Edited by: Benita van Eyssen

articles.title: Alleged KillSec Ransomware Mastermind a 16-Year-Old - Dark Reading
articles.summary: Alleged KillSec Ransomware Mastermind a 16-Year-Old  Dark Reading
articles.full_text:
Law enforcement from multiple countries collaborated to disrupt a cybercrime operation that has claimed some 500 victims worldwide in the past two years.
German authorities have identified a 16-year-old as the alleged mastermind of the KillSec ransomware operation, following a coordinated law enforcement operation that resulted in the arrests of three suspects and searches of eight properties in Spain, Greece, Romania, and the UK.
In an Oct. 1 statement, Hamburg police said investigators also took control of KillSec's leak website and secured at least 110TB of data to prevent further unauthorized access.
"Operation KillSwitch" Cybercrime Takedown
The developments stem from "Operation KillSwitch," an international investigation that German law enforcement led into roughly 1,000 suspected KillSec cyberattacks worldwide, at least 70 of which involved government organizations. Investigators have so far confirmed about 500 of those attacks to be successful.
Authorities from multiple countries, including Germany, the United States, the United Kingdom, Spain, Romania, and Greece, took part in the investigation. Europol and Eurojust coordinated the international effort, while cybersecurity firms Bitdefender and Group-IB provided technical support.
"The coordinated action targeted both the people behind KillSec and the systems they relied on," Europol said in a press statement. Authorities raided eight homes across four countries, provisionally arrested three individuals, and took control of five servers and other infrastructure that KillSec was using to manage its activities and store victim data, it added. "Authorities also took control of domains operated by KillSec and redirected visitors to a law enforcement seizure notice."
Reuters described the 16-year-old as a Romanian national who was arrested in the Spanish city of Alicante. Reuters quoted a Europol spokesman as describing the teen as the "administrator" of the KillSec operation. Separately, the US Justice Department indicted Dutch national Fouad Eltibrizi for his alleged role related to the KillSec operation. Meanwhile, police in the UK arrested Eltibrizi (aka "Archduke") on Sept. 30 and are preparing to extradite him to the US, where he will face charges related to unauthorized computer access conspiracy. He faces a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison if convicted.
Suspect Orchestrated Opportunistic Ransomware Attacks
KillSec is a prolific ransomware group that surfaced in 2024 and became known for exploiting known vulnerabilities and poorly secured access points, particularly in cloud environments, to gain access to enterprise systems and exfiltrate data. The group then used its leak site to publicly name victims and threaten to publish stolen files unless they paid a ransom, says Alexandru Nicola Stoica, senior threat researcher at Bitdefender DracoTeam, in comments to Dark Reading. Investigators also found evidence that the group used AI to build and maintain its infrastructure and identify potential victims, Stoica says.
Bitdefender, which has tracked KillSec since 2024, provided technical assistance, infrastructure mapping, and continuous monitoring support for Operation KillSwitch for more than a year, Stoica says. The company has observed nearly 300 victims appearing on KillSec's leak site since the company began tracking the threat actor.
"The group posted 126 victims in 2025 and 25 in 2026, the most recent on Sept. 18, 12 days before action day on the last leak site they used," Stoica says, but cautions that leak-site counts do not necessarily reflect the actual number of victims claimed by a threat actor. "KillSec is mostly opportunistic with its targets," he adds, "and we don't have an estimate of losses" to victims.

An international law enforcement operation dubbed “Operation KillSwitch” seized the KillSec ransomware gang’s data leak site and servers, led to three arrests, and identified a 16-year-old as the group’s alleged administrator.
The coordinated law enforcement action was carried out on September 30, involving authorities from Belgium, the United States, Finland, Germany, Greece, the Netherlands, Romania, Spain, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom.
Europol and Eurojust also took part in the investigation, along with cybersecurity companies Bitdefender and Group-IB.
"The action was part of Operation KillSwitch, an international investigation led by German authorities into around 1,000 suspected attacks worldwide," says Europol.
"Investigators identified a 16-year-old as the group’s suspected main operator. Three suspects were provisionally arrested and eight properties searched in Greece, Romania, Spain, and the United Kingdom. Authorities also targeted the group’s criminal proceeds."
The investigation began in 2025 and helped law enforcement identify suspects believed to be an administrator, developer, negotiator, and affiliate of the cybercrime group.
According to Europol, the suspected administrator and main operator of KillSec is only 16 years old. Another suspected member, described as a developer, turned 18 in August 2026 and was still a minor when some of the alleged crimes were committed.
Authorities have also identified individuals suspected of being a negotiator and an affiliate.
Hamburg Police said it investigated the group's server infrastructure, which led to the identification and shutdown of five servers, including KillSec's main server and several servers allegedly used to store stolen data.
One of the seized sites is KillSec's dark web data leak site, hosted at https://ks5424y3wpr5zlug5c7i6svvxweinhbdcqcfnptkfcutrncfazzgz5id.onion/, which now contains a seizure message.
"The domain, servers and all associated data linked to Operation KillSwitch have been taken into control by State Criminal Police Office of Hamburg and international law enforcement agencies," reads the seizure banner.
Clicking the seizure banner leads to the Operation KillSwitch website, which includes a law-enforcement video about the ransomware gang and the arrests.
During the operation, law enforcement also seized at least 110 terabytes of stolen data to prevent continued unauthorized access, and conducted eight searches in Greece, Romania, Spain, and the United Kingdom and provisionally arrested three suspects.
Investigators have so far determined that around 500 of KillSec’s attacks were successful, though authorities cautioned that the numbers could change as they continue to analyze seized evidence.
At least 70 of the suspected attacks are linked to organizations in Germany, including 18 cases connected to Hamburg.
KillSec has been active since around 2024 and is accused of exploiting software vulnerabilities and poorly secured edge devices and platforms to breach corporate systems and steal sensitive data.
The threat actors used the stolen corporate data to extort victims via KillSec’s dark web leak site, with threats that the data would be published if a ransom was not paid.
Europol says that KillSec received "substantial" ransom payments from these data-theft attacks.
Investigators also discovered that members of the group used artificial intelligence to help build and maintain their ransomware infrastructure and identify potential victims.
Authorities are now examining seized computers, servers, and other data while attempting to trace KillSec's alleged criminal proceeds, including cryptocurrency.
Investigators say the seized evidence could reveal further victims, attacks, and people involved with the ransomware operation.

A Republican senator was warned that his facts were “unvetted” before his attempt to discredit former special counsel Jack Smith unraveled into a viral gaffe, according to a new report.
During a congressional hearing on Monday, Missouri Senator Eric Schmitt accused Smith of secretly meeting with Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis at an NBA game in Georgia. Both Smith and Willis had overseen investigations into President Donald Trump’s attempts to overturn the 2020 election.
But Schmitt’s allegation rested on an apparent mix-up between the Atlanta Hawks and the Iowa Hawkeyes during the hearing to the visible shock of onlookers.
Prior to the blunder, Schmitt had sought Justice Department material that might establish a link between the two investigations, sources told MS NOW. The request came amid a broader GOP effort to portray the criminal probes into Trump as highly coordinated witch hunts.
Schmitt was later given access to text messages related to Smith. But committee staff “explicitly warned Schmitt's team that the texts were unvetted and that it was their responsibility to verify the information,” the outlet reported.
What followed was an embarrassing moment, broadcast live to viewers across the country.
During his questioning, Schmitt said he had obtained text messages showing Smith attended a Hawks game in Atlanta on February 3, 2024. When Smith appeared confused and said he had not been at the game, Schmitt replied: “I think you’ve already perjured yourself.”
His aides then briefly held up a poster board that appeared to show text messages indicating seats had been reserved for Smith.
Schmitt concluded by calling Smith a “villain” and a “total dirtbag” who “weaponized the Department of Justice against political enemies to an extent that has never happened in the history of this country.”
Soon after, Smith suggested he understood the apparent mix-up. He said he had attended a women’s college basketball game in Maryland around the time frame Schmitt described — Iowa’s Hawkeyes playing the University of Maryland.
Senator Amy Klobuchar, a Minnesota Democrat, also came to Smith’s defense, criticizing Schmitt for leveling accusations without first verifying the facts.
“That might be the confusion over the names of the team,” Klobuchar said. “But perhaps you should’ve looked at it more carefully.”
“I think that people should have their facts straight before they accuse someone of being a dirtbag and not get the teams wrong,” she added.
Schmitt later said he did not regret his questioning, telling Politico that Smith “has lied before to Congress.”
Smith’s two federal cases against Trump — one involving alleged election interference and the other classified documents — were dismissed after Trump won the 2024 election.
The Georgia case brought by Willis stalled after the Georgia Court of Appeals removed Willis from the prosecution in December 2024, citing the appearance of impropriety stemming from her relationship with a special prosecutor. A subsequent prosecutor ultimately declined to pursue the case.

articles.title: Putin warns West that Russia is prepared to use ‘all weapons’ to protect Kaliningrad - CNN
articles.summary: Putin warns West that Russia is prepared to use ‘all weapons’ to protect Kaliningrad  CNNRussia warns NATO of a possible nuclear response if Kaliningrad is cut off  apnews.comPutin warns West that Russia is ready to use every weapon to protect Kaliningrad  BBCPutin says ‘all weapons at disposal’ if there’s an attack on Russia – as it happened  The GuardianWhy Russia's Kaliningrad is a potential flashpoint with NATO  Reuters
articles.full_text:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has warned the West against escalating the war in Ukraine, saying Moscow is prepared to use “all weapons” in its arsenal — including nuclear — if its Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad comes under attack.
Speaking at the Valdai Discussion Club in Moscow on Thursday, the Russian leader said he had no plans to attack any European country but was prepared to respond to Western aggression if necessary and referenced the Russian territory sandwiched between NATO members Poland and Lithuania.
His warning follows recent military drills by NATO near Kaliningrad that the bloc has described as defensive exercises to strengthen deterrence. Those exercises have prompted strong concerns from Moscow, which warned in late September it would retaliate if NATO attempted to blockade the exclave by air or sea.
“The drills in the Baltic Sea, following one another … Then the attempts to arrest our ships and vessels. All this is an escalation. And then we began to hear statements regarding the Kaliningrad region,” Putin said.
“If it comes to direct attack against the Russian Federation, in this case on Kaliningrad and possibly some other territories, of course the issue of using all weapons in our country’s arsenal will inevitably and unavoidably emerge on the agenda. This is unavoidable,” he cautioned.
NATO, several European countries and the United Kingdom have accused Russia of conducting hybrid warfare against them, including cyberattacks, sabotage and espionage attempts, aimed at breaking their support for Ukraine.
Russia’s war in Ukraine, dubbed by Moscow as a “special military operation,” is now in its fifth year, but Putin shows no sign of slowing his offensive and has instead intensified strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and its capital city of Kyiv ahead of an anticipated bitterly cold winter.
But recent Ukrainian drone strikes on Russia’s oil refineries have led to widespread fuel shortages, shattering the illusion that the consequences of the conflict are far removed from ordinary Russians.
Long queues of cars at fuel stations have been seen in major cities, while hits on Russia’s largest online retailers have increased pressure on the already strained wartime economy.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky regularly refers to Ukrainian drone strikes deep inside Russian territory as “long-range sanctions,” designed to reduce Russia’s revenues, military capacity and push the Kremlin into negotiations.
In his speech Thursday to foreign policy and international affairs academics, Putin admitted the Ukrainian strikes were taking a toll on Russia’s economy, saying they had cost Russia 1% of its gross domestic product (GDP) and that Ukrainian military maneuvers in the Black Sea have taken out over 100 Russian ships.
However, Putin also made clear he remains undeterred.
“In the Black Sea — that’s a combat zone; we struck military vessels and ships transporting military cargo, and we hardly ever made a mistake. Throughout this whole saga, they [Ukraine] have knocked out over 100 of our ships. Well, we started hitting back, and now we’re being bombarded from every direction with appeals: “Oh, please stop doing that,” Putin said.
“It’s the same story with our oil refineries; they (Ukraine) openly declared their goal was to damage our economy. Did they succeed? Partially — by our estimates, we lost about one percent of our GDP. And it was done deliberately — these are civilian targets, after all. Well, they got a mirror-image response,” Putin added, sidestepping that it was Moscow who launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Putin’s admission of the economic toll comes just one day after he told newly elected members of the State Duma — the lower house of Russia’s parliament, which predictably saw the United Russia party that backs Putin hold onto its majority — that the Russian economy was stable.
Taking the opportunity to swipe at Ukraine, the Russian president on Wednesday derided Kyiv’s reliance on financial assistance from its Western allies.
“Mistakes, especially now, are absolutely unacceptable,” he warned parliamentarians. “Unlike some, and we won’t point fingers, Russia can’t run around the world humiliating (itself) by begging for handouts with an outstretched hand,” he said.
“Firstly, because, as I have already said, it is humiliating. Secondly, no one is going to give us anything, and we know that very well. And thirdly, and most importantly, we do not need it. Russia’s financial system and economy are secure,” he continued.
While signaling in recent weeks that he does not intend to draw back from the war in Ukraine, Putin also said he would prefer the conflict to end through talks.
Ahead of the election, Putin had said the results would show Russians are united by the military and its goals — though the Levada Center, an independent pollster, found in an August poll that 59% of Russians favored moving to peace talks.
In a further sign that Putin does not plan to slow down the “special military operation,” budget documents reviewed by Reuters show that Russia plans to spend 17.1 trillion rubles ($205.112 billion) on defense in 2027, about 27% more than originally budgeted and the highest level since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

articles.title: Mounting pressure on Iran could lead to attack on Israel, ex-national security council head warns - The Jerusalem Post
articles.summary: Mounting pressure on Iran could lead to attack on Israel, ex-national security council head warns  The Jerusalem Post
articles.full_text:
Former national security council head Meir Ben-Shabbat warned that mounting pressure on Iran could still push Tehran toward a direct attack on Israel, while arguing that a future agreement between Washington and Tehran could provide the Iranian regime with a strategic lifeline, he told Maariv in a Wednesday interview.
Ben-Shabbat, who was among the architects of the Abraham Accords, said the Iranian regime remained under severe pressure but had not yet reached a point of desperation.
“First, regarding Iran’s situation: despite the challenging reality it faces, the impression is that the regime in Tehran still does not have its back against the wall. In medical terms, its condition is serious but not critical.
In any event, Israel must always be prepared on the assumption that at a certain point in time, which will not necessarily be possible to predict, Iran will consider attacking it,” he said.
Ben-Shabbat also warned that a US agreement with Iran could have serious strategic consequences regardless of whether it formally restricted Israel’s freedom of action.
“Israel’s freedom of action to defend itself against an existential threat is a matter about which there is no dispute. The consequences of an agreement with Iran are very severe even if they do not have an effect on Israel’s freedom of action," he said.
"Any agreement with the Iranians, even if it meets the parameters set by the American administration, will ultimately be a lifeline for the regime in Tehran; it will finance its recovery and preserve the dangers from it."
"This clear and unequivocal position was voiced a few days ago by Gen. Jack Keane, who served as vice chief of staff of the US Army and received the Presidential Medal from Trump. He precisely defined the strategic trap placed before the American president and recommended making the creation of conditions that put the Iranian regime on a path to collapse a goal. Any additional word is unnecessary.”
Iran has been waging a campaign against Europe 'for some time'
Asked whether an attempted attack on RAF Fairford, if linked to Iran or one of its proxies, would indicate that Tehran was expanding its campaign against the West into Europe, Ben-Shabbat said Iran had already been waging such a campaign for some time.
“Iran has been waging a campaign against Europe for some time. I remind you that Iran has already attacked European bases: Iranian UAVs, apparently launched from Lebanon by Hezbollah, directly struck the British Air Force base at Akrotiri in Cyprus.
"The confrontation between Iran and European countries is admittedly not being conducted as a frontal conventional war, but it certainly exists as a multidimensional hybrid campaign combining warfare in the ‘gray zone,’ terrorism through proxies, cyberattacks, and economic influence. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said in June 2025 that Israel ‘is doing the dirty work for all of us’ in reference to the campaign against Iran. He was right then, and his words are also correct today.”
Asked whether Israelis and Jews abroad should prepare for an increase in attempts to target them amid rising pressure on Iran, Ben-Shabbat replied: “The system and the citizens must assume so.”
Netanyahu's visit to the UAE tightens important relationship
Ben-Shabbat also addressed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s reported secret visit to the United Arab Emirates, saying coordination with Abu Dhabi was particularly important given the possibility of either military escalation with Iran or a diplomatic agreement.
“I remind you that we are in the midst of the confrontation with Iran, with on the one hand – a possibility of military escalation, and on the other hand – a possibility of a diplomatic arrangement. A common position and alignment by Israel and the Emirates are things that require discussion and coordination.”
On the possibility of expanding the Abraham Accords, including through Saudi normalization, Ben-Shabbat said the current regional uncertainty reduced the chances of a breakthrough.
“In general, the chances of this during periods of uncertainty, election campaigns or fighting, are not high. Israel’s value as a security and technological-economic partner is clear. Israeli's interest in expanding the agreements is clear, but it must come from Israeli strength. Under no circumstances should we court them or pay compensation.”
When will the Hezbollah conflict be over?
Turning to Lebanon, Ben-Shabbat said Hezbollah had suffered a strategic blow but that the campaign against the group was far from over.
“The pager operation and the Israeli attack that followed it two years ago were a turning point in the war between Israel and Hezbollah, which led to the elimination of the person who had ruled southern Lebanon and the Shi’ite terrorist organization for 40 years, cut off Iran’s strongest and most important proxy arm that it had in the region, enabled the collapse of the Assad regime and the shattering of the perception of Syria as Iran’s backyard, and created significant shock waves in the Middle East.
“Above and below the surface, the signs of the change that occurred can be seen in every field: Hezbollah lost the control it had over the territory and the line of villages along the border with Israel, it also lost commanders, fighters, infrastructure, and strategic assets; and beyond that, its status in the Lebanese arena.
"Naim Qassem is finding it difficult to step into Nasrallah’s shoes and fill the military, political, or social vacuum he left behind. Lebanese voices expressing deep frustration over the heavy price of Hezbollah’s war, which is not necessarily Lebanon’s war, are growing, and alongside all of these – the Lebanese government, despite its weakness, is trying to establish a new order.
“The Lebanese-American researcher and commentator Hussein Abd al-Hussein determined in an article he published recently that Hezbollah suffered a strategic defeat but refuses to acknowledge it. From Israel’s point of view, these are significant achievements, but the work is not complete and it is too early for summaries.
"All the players in the system understand that the way Iran emerges from the current confrontation will directly shape Hezbollah’s power, status, and future policy. Therefore, Israel must tighten its control over the areas it has defined, maintain a continuous offensive initiative, block every attempt at renewed force buildup, and not ease the pressure on the enemy’s throat for even a moment.”
Israel continues to strive to destroy Hamas
Ben-Shabbat rejected the idea that Israel had shifted from seeking to destroy Hamas to merely weakening the organization.
“I am not aware of a change in the goals of the war regarding Gaza, and in my opinion there is no room for such a change. Determination, patience, and persistence are the key to success. Israel must complete the task until the military and governing capabilities of the Hamas organization in the Strip are completely eliminated, the territory is completely demilitarized, and there is Israeli security control.
"From the perspective of the State of Israel, it is not enough to settle only for removing the security threat; it should have an interest in the area in which the cruel monster that carried out the October 7 massacre grew, becoming eternal testimony to the prices that anyone who thinks in the future about attacking Israel will pay.”
Asked about European measures targeting goods from the West Bank, east Jerusalem, and the Golan Heights, and their possible economic impact on Palestinians, Ben-Shabbat said he did not have the exact figures but accused some international actors of prioritizing pressure on Israeli settlements over Palestinian economic welfare.
“I am not familiar with the precise economic data, but among some of the players in the international system, the desire to harm the settlement enterprise in Judea and Samaria outweighs the interest in ensuring the economic well-being of the Palestinians there. This is another expression of the double standard and hypocrisy on their part.”
Turkey: A growing power in the Middle East
Ben-Shabbat also focused on Turkey, which he described as a growing regional power taking advantage of changes in Syria, Africa, and the eastern Mediterranean.
“The Greek defense minister, Nikos Dendias, said a few months ago: ‘If we ask the United States and Turkey how they see the future of the world and the region in ten years, we will receive two completely opposite answers – and that is the whole story.’ His words capture the abyss between the American vision and Erdogan’s ambitions for the Middle East and the international system.
“More than any other country, Turkey knows how to exploit global great-power competition and the changes in the Middle East in order to establish its status as a dominant regional power. It dances at every wedding and collects diplomatic brokerage fees from all the players. Following the collapse of the Assad regime and the forced withdrawal of the Iranian military presence, Turkey became the dominant player in Syria. From local territorial control in northern Syria, it moved to exercising broad influence across the entire country.
“Syria is only part of Erdogan’s broader vision of ‘neo-Ottomanism.’ He seeks to restore Turkey to the status of a regional superpower and expand its influence far beyond its official borders. source_detail.name: United States Mission to the United Nations (.gov)

articles.full_text:
Ambassador Mike Waltz
U.S. Representative to the United Nations
New York, New York
AS PREPARED
Thank you, Mr. President.
On September 17, Russia and China vetoed a resolution to extend the mandate of the Panel of Experts that supports the 1737 Committee.
Those who vetoed this Resolution love to lecture all of us on their love for the UN Charter and this institution.
Well, let’s read a bit of the UN Charter. Article 25 requires members to “accept and carry out” Council decisions. The 1737 Committee exists for exactly that purpose: to help Member States carry out sanctions agreed to at the Council—through Resolution 1737.
Russia and China once understood this. In fact, they voted for every one of the six Security Council resolutions whose provisions snapped back last year.
Resolution 1696, which demanded Iran suspend all uranium enrichment and reprocessing;
Resolution 1737, which imposed nuclear- and missile-related restrictions and asset freezes after Iran failed to comply;
Resolution 1747, which prohibited Iran from exporting arms and expanded sanctions after Iran failed to comply again;
Resolution 1803, which tightened nuclear restrictions and expanded financial and travel measures against Iran following still more noncompliance;
Resolution 1835, which again demanded that Iran comply with the Council’s previous resolutions and meet the IAEA’s requirements;
Resolution 1929, which imposed new arms and missile restrictions and established the Panel of Experts to monitor it all;
And, finally Resolution 2231, which created the mechanism for all those measures to snap back if Iran went back on its word and pursued a nuclear weapon again.
Russia and China voted for every single one.
Now, while Iran attacks its neighbors and continues to seek a nuclear weapon—all in blatant violation of numerous Security Council Resolutions—where are Russia and China?
Today, they’ll tell you sanctions against Iran haven’t “snapped back.” They’ll tell you the sanctions aren’t valid or that they don’t exist.
But the UN’s own sanctions website is abundantly clear. It reads: sanctions were re-applied on September 27, 2025.
That came after France, Germany, and the United Kingdom spent years exhausting diplomatic options and giving Iran repeated chances to return to compliance. It didn’t.
So the E3 triggered the snapback process. The Council considered whether sanctions relief should continue. The Council did not extend that relief—and, exactly as Resolution 2231 provided, the previous UN sanctions automatically came back into force.
Why? Well, Iran broke the rules. They refused to abandon their nuclear ambitions—enriching uranium to 60% which has no credible civilian purpose.
Just ask the IAEA, whose inspectors are repeatedly denied access in Iran and whose Board of Governors referred Iran to the Security Council for non-compliance just two weeks ago.
Or, ask Iranian negotiators, who still refuse to give up their nuclear program even as their nation crumbles.
And, now there are those on the Security Council who have chosen to not only look the other way—but to defang some of the only teeth this institution has.
And it isn’t just about Iran. Russia vetoed renewals of the North Korea and Mali panels, while China abstained. Russia and China have also obstructed expert appointments for the Central African Republic and Yemen panels.
Colleagues, you’ve got to ask yourself: why? I’ll let you decide for yourselves, but consider this:
We know that Iran exported arms and related materiel to Russia, Venezuela under the Maduro regime, and countries in Africa. We also have information that Russia transferred fighter aircraft and armored vehicles to Iran in late 2025.
Colleagues, these are precisely the activities independent experts should investigate.
This is why the United States will continue to advocate for a Panel of Experts—while advancing an independent, multilateral panel to monitor and report on global compliance with the sanctions on Iran that the Security Council agreed to through all six of the resolutions that snapped back last year.
We look forward to working with partners, on and off the Council, to realize this initiative. Blocking UN monitors must not block scrutiny. We urge every country that values this institution to support this effort.
Thank you, Mr. President.
###

articles.title: Microsoft study says United States has become the Worlds most targeted Country for Cyber Attacks - Cybersecurity Insiders
articles.summary: Microsoft study says United States has become the Worlds most targeted Country for Cyber Attacks  Cybersecurity Insiders
articles.full_text:
The United States has emerged as the world’s most targeted country for cyberattacks, according to Microsoft Annual Cyber Defense Report. The report highlights the growing scale and sophistication of global cyber threats, with the United States accounting for the largest share of cyber activity observed during the reporting period.
According to the report, the United States accounted for approximately 25.5% of global cyber activity, making it the most targeted country worldwide. Israel ranked second with 7.6%, followed by Ukraine at 4.8% and Taiwan at 3.9%. The figures underline how geopolitical tensions, military conflicts and strategic interests are increasingly influencing the global cyber threat landscape.
Israel’s position is particularly significant, as the country not only ranked second globally among the most targeted nations but also emerged as the most targeted country in the Middle East and Africa region. The concentration of cyber activity against Israel reflects the wider impact of ongoing regional conflicts and heightened tensions involving state and non-state actors.
Microsoft also highlighted the growing role of artificial intelligence (AI) in cyber operations. While AI is increasingly being used to strengthen cybersecurity defenses, threat actors are also exploiting the technology to make attacks faster, more sophisticated and more difficult to detect. According to the report, AI is being incorporated into large-scale phishing campaigns and other malicious activities, including attacks involving increasingly autonomous AI agents.
Among the major state-linked cyber threats, Iran remains a significant actor. Microsoft’s findings indicate that between July 2025 and June 2026, Iranian cyber activity was primarily focused on Israel, followed by the United States. The targeting patterns were linked to heightened geopolitical tensions and military escalations involving countries in and around the Strait of Hormuz, an important strategic waterway for global energy supplies.
The objectives behind these cyber campaigns extended beyond conventional financial cybercrime. Microsoft identified espionage, intelligence gathering, support for kinetic military operations, foreign influence and data destruction among the major motivations behind sophisticated attacks.
Ransomware and other forms of destructive malware also continued to pose a serious threat. In addition to targeting government and corporate data, attackers increasingly focused on critical infrastructure and operational technology. The energy, telecommunications and manufacturing sectors were among the areas facing significant attention from cyber campaigners.
The findings demonstrate that cyberattacks are increasingly becoming an extension of geopolitical conflicts. As governments, businesses and critical infrastructure become more digitally connected, cyber operations can potentially disrupt essential services without requiring traditional physical attacks.
Microsoft’s report therefore underscores the need for stronger cybersecurity preparedness, improved threat intelligence and greater cooperation between governments and private-sector organizations. At the same time, the rapid development of AI means that cybersecurity strategies will need to evolve continuously to address increasingly automated and sophisticated threats.

articles.title: Seoul warns 'further action' if Ukraine does not apologise over prisoner-of-war row - BBC
articles.summary: Seoul warns 'further action' if Ukraine does not apologise over prisoner-of-war row  BBCSouth Korea's Lee threatens action against Ukraine over transfer of North Korean soldiers  ReutersRow between Ukraine, South Korea mounts over North Korean POWs  Al JazeeraSeoul suspects Zelenskyy revealed North Korean POW transfer to win arms support  Euronews.comHow a humanitarian transfer of North Korean POWs became a row between Seoul and Kyiv  Korea Joong...
articles.full_text:
South Korea's President Lee Jae Myung has threatened to take unspecified "further action" if Ukraine does not issue a public apology for revealing that two North Korean prisoners of war had been sent to the South.
Ukraine's leader Volodymyr Zelensky made the disclosure to the UN general assembly last week, angering Seoul, who said the move was meant to stay secret.
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha on Thursday described the situation as a "diplomatic misunderstanding", adding that Kyiv was "working" to resolve it.
Lee rejected this characterisation on X, saying it concerned "the dignity of the Korean people and the nation".
Lee's office said last week that it was Ukraine that requested for the move to be kept secret, partly to protect the North Koreans' families, and also because Kyiv wanted to avoid criticism that it had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners of war.
Zelensky's office responded, saying the two countries had no such agreement to keep the move confidential, further escalating the situation.
Lee himself faced heavy criticism at home after Zelensky's disclosure, with the South Korean opposition accusing him of covering up the transfer to appease Pyongyang.
The two soldiers, who were among thousands of North Koreans supporting Russia in the Ukraine war, had earlier told local media they wanted to be sent to South Korea.
Speaking to Ukrainian media on Thursday, Sybiha, the foreign minister, said he "hopes that this situation will be resolved in the very near future".
"We are working on it. For us, South Korea is an important country. And I really hope for momentum, continuation, and concrete results that we are truly achieving with them," he said.
Lee, in response, accused Kyiv of attempting to "bring war on the Korean Peninsula".
"We express serious regret that, instead of acknowledging the facts of the agreement and apologising, they are talking about an imminent military clash between the North and South," he said in an X post.
Seoul has been sympathetic to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion, but has adhered to its longstanding policy of not providing lethal weapons to any country engaged in active war.

Vladimir Putin has said Russia will use all the weapons at their disposal if the country is attacked by Europe in his latest sabre-rattling threat.
The Russian president reiterated Moscow's long-held position that Russia is not planning to attack European countries, but said it would respond to any attacks with all its arsenal.
“If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation — in this case we mean Kaliningrad, or maybe some other territories — of course, inevitably and immediately the question of Russian Federation using all weapons at the disposal of our country will appear on the agenda,” Putin said.
It comes as several Russian embassies in Europe this week issued statements that said Moscow has “information that NATO is preparing (an) air and naval blockade of Kaliningrad and (the) Kaliningrad region”. They provided no evidence to support such a claim.
“There should be no mistake — Russia would be ready to use all its arsenal, including nuclear weapons, to defend its territory if NATO countries try to isolate (the) Kaliningrad region from the rest of the country,” the Russian Embassy in Ireland said in its statement on Tuesday.
South Korea threatens to escalate row with Ukraine over POWs
South Korean president Lee Jae Myung says Seoul will take additional measures if Ukraine continues to deny the existence of a confidentiality agreement related to the repatriation of North Korean prisoners of war, and called on Kyiv to acknowledge the agreement and apologise.
In a post on X, Lee also expressed grave regret over Ukraine's response, accusing Kyiv of undermining South Korea's head of state and warning that remarks about an imminent military clash between North and South Korea amounted to invoking the risk of war on the Korean Peninsula.
Russian air strikes hit Southern Bridge in Kyiv again, says mayor
Russian air strikes have again hit the Southern Bridge in the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv, mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram on Friday.
On Thursday, Russian drones smashed into a school in Kyiv and into the Southern Bridge over the Dnipro River, triggering fires in the capital, as Moscow continues its near-daily around-the-clock strikes on Ukraine.
Kanye West’s Russia concerts cancelled after weeks of uncertainty
The 49-year-old American rapper was scheduled to perform at the Gazprom Arena in St Petersburg on 10 and 11 October.
Writing on the messaging platform Telegram, Moscow-based promoter Say Agency announced that the dates had been scrapped.
"Friends, it is with sincere regret that we inform you that the Ye concerts in Saint Petersburg on the scheduled dates will not be able to take place," the agency posted.
Watch: Ukraine strikes two ships linked to Russia in Black Sea, Zelensky says
Russia intensifies airstrikes
Russia has intensified airstrikes as its overall frontline advances have slowed this year.
One person was wounded on Thursday in a Russian attack on a business centre in the Black Sea port city of Odesa, regional officials said.
City administration chief Serhiy Lysak said infrastructure had been damaged but gave no further details.
Odesa and the surrounding region have been a frequent target of attacks aimed partly at choking Kyiv's export revenues.
Russia, which says it strikes only military targets, reported that it had attacked a data centre in Odesa and a cargo vessel in the nearby port of Chornomorsk.
Ukraine has also stepped up attacks on Russia, striking oil refineries and major online retailers to try to undermine Moscow's war effort.
One man was killed when a Ukrainian drone exploded in the town of Graivoron in Russia's Belgorod region, local authorities said on Thursday.
Merz warns of more Russian hybrid attacks as he reaffirms support for Ukraine
Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned on Thursday that Germany faced more hybrid attacks from Russia as he pledged to continue support for Ukraine ahead of what is likely to be its harshest winter since the start of Russia's invasion in 2022.
German authorities have warned repeatedly that Russia is conducting a hybrid campaign of drone and cyber attacks, accusing Moscow of being behind an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport in August.
"We are preparing for further hybrid attacks, including serious ones," Merz said in a speech marking the award of the 2026 Westphalian Peace Prize to the NATO alliance.
Moscow has rejected the accusations from Western governments and intelligence services.Speaking to a forum of Russia experts on Thursday, President Vladimir Putin said Moscow was not about to attack foreign factories that produce weapons for Ukraine but that this was something Russian intelligence services needed to track closely.
Merz and his conservatives have been badly weakened by elections in two eastern German states last month in which the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) triumphed.
Putin says he will use ‘all Russia’s weapons’ against Europe if attacked in chilling threat
Vladimir Putin has said Russia will use all the weapons at their disposal in response to European aggression.
The Russian president reiterated Moscow's long-held position that Russia is not planning to attack European countries, but would respond to any attacks with all its arsenal.
“If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation — in this case we mean Kaliningrad, or maybe some other territories — of course, inevitably and immediately the question of Russian Federation using all weapons at the disposal of our country will appear on the agenda,” Putin said.
It comes as several Russian embassies in Europe this week issued statements that said Moscow has “information that NATO is preparing (an) air and naval blockade of Kaliningrad and (the) Kaliningrad region.”
They accused European leaders of “playing a dangerous game” by saying Russia might attack another country or ramp up a campaign of destabilising attacks with drones and sabotage. Moscow has called the allegations absurd.
Watch: Ukraine strikes two ships linked to Russia in Black Sea, Zelensky says
Putin says Western companies could get their Russian assets back
Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Thursday that Western companies could get their Russian assets back if "a favourable scenario" came to pass.
Speaking at the Valdai Forum of international experts, Putin said: "We have not nationalised anything from anyone. Yes, we are placing certain enterprises under external administration. 
“But in some European countries, they have simply, in a blatant breach of every conceivable and inconceivable rule, seized huge enterprises from us – for example, in the Federal Republic of Germany.”
Exclusive: UK’s top military chief: Large-scale war in Europe means our security cannot be taken for granted
The head of the UK military has warned that Europe must take greater responsibility for its own defence as war returns to the continent and shows that security can no longer be taken for granted.
Writing for The Independent, Air Chief Marshal Sir Richard Knighton, the UK chief of the defence staff, and his Swedish counterpart General Michael Claesson urged the need to reinforce Nato’s northern flank in the face of new threats and “reckless acts of aggression” from abroad.
The warning came just days after Sweden and Finland scrambled fighter jets together for the first time to intercept Russian military aircraft, while the United States is reportedly considering pulling nearly a third of its forces out of Europe.

articles.full_text:
Moscow ordered Hungarian embassy and consulate staff out just weeks after Budapest expelled 10 Russian diplomats on national security grounds in September, the first such move by Hungary since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Russia expelled a group of Hungarian diplomats on Thursday after Hungary ordered 10 Russian diplomats out last month, marking a sharp break from the era of former Premier Viktor Orbán, who maintained closer ties with Moscow than any other EU leader.
Hungary's chargé d'affaires Gábor Gergics was summoned to Russia's foreign ministry and informed that staff from the Hungarian embassy in Moscow and consulates in St Petersburg and Kazan had been ordered to leave within two weeks.
Moscow described Hungary's original 8 September expulsion as a "baseless and openly unfriendly" act.
Budapest acknowledged Moscow's decision but said it stood by its position.
"Hungary is not interested in an escalation of diplomatic tensions. But we stand by our decision, taken on national security grounds. Our missions continue to operate in full, and Hungary will maintain its diplomatic presence in Russia," the Hungarian foreign ministry wrote on X.
Foreign Minister Anita Orbán said at the time of the initial expulsion that the Russian diplomats "had been engaged in activities in Hungary that are unacceptable for diplomats under the Vienna Convention."
The mutual expulsions follow a shift in Hungarian foreign policy since Prime Minister Péter Magyar took office earlier this year.
At the end of August, the new government's guidance to its delegation at the UN General Assembly officially described Russia as a threat to Hungary and to the "global order," condemned its ongoing all-out war in Ukraine and affirmed support for Ukrainian sovereignty and its right to self-defence.
Hungary is also seeking to improve relations with Kyiv, although Budapest is blocking the opening of new EU accession negotiation clusters with Ukraine to secure concessions on the rights of the country's Hungarian minority.
Orbán, who was in power for 16 years until his party Fidesz' loss in general elections this April, openly sympathised with the Kremlin and refused to join other EU member states in expelling Russian diplomats after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
He made multiple visits to Moscow after the invasion and repeatedly used Hungary's veto in the European Council to block Ukraine-related initiatives.
Magyar has promised "pragmatic" relations with Moscow during his tenure.

articles.full_text:
Cisco released security updates to address a critical zero-day in the Catalyst SD-WAN Manager (tracked as CVE-2026-76504) that attackers are actively exploiting to escalate to admin privileges.
Formerly known as SD-WAN vManage, Catalyst SD-WAN Manager is network management software that lets admins monitor and manage up to 6,000 SD-WAN devices from a single dashboard.
"In September 2026, the Cisco PSIRT became aware of active exploitation of this vulnerability," the company warned on Wednesday. "Cisco strongly recommends that customers upgrade to a fixed software release to remediate this vulnerability."
The CVE-2026-76504 vulnerability affects all deployments regardless of system configuration, was found in API session-based authentication management, and allows unauthenticated attackers to access vulnerable systems remotely with admin privileges.
"This vulnerability is due to improper handling of URI encoding in an HTTP request, which allows the request to bypass an authentication rule that is intended to restrict access to a specific API endpoint," Cisco added.
"An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a crafted HTTP request to the API of the affected system."
While the company didn't share further details regarding attacks exploiting CVE-2026-76504, it shared indicators of compromise (IOCs) warning admins that threat actors are using %6a as the URI-encoded character "j" in malicious requests.
It also advised security teams investigating potentially compromised SD-WAN systems to check the serviceproxy-access.log file located under /var/log/nms/containers/service-proxy and the vmanage-server.log file under /var/log/nms/for entries related to j_security_check from unknown or unauthorized IP addresses.
"For help determining if a Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager has been compromised, customers may open a case with the Cisco TAC," it added, advising admins first to collect admin-tech files to support the review.

articles.title: Europe faces defense vulnerability window until 2030, Dutch military chief warns - streamlinefeed.co.ke
articles.summary: Europe faces defense vulnerability window until 2030, Dutch military chief warns  streamlinefeed.co.ke
articles.full_text:
Europe faces a critical window of military vulnerability that will persist until 2030, driven by a dangerous gap between escalating security threats and the slow pace of defense procurement, according to the head of the Dutch armed forces.
Speaking at the Euronews Defence and Space Summit in Brussels, General Onno Eichelsheim, Chief of Defence of the Netherlands, warned that European nations must urgently abandon fragmented national strategies in favor of unified industrial cooperation to close the readiness gap.
The 2030 Readiness Gap
General Eichelsheim cautioned that immediate geopolitical threats currently outpace the delivery of modern military capabilities. While European defense spending has surged following the invasion of Ukraine, the actual deployment of advanced equipment remains constrained by bureaucratic delays and protectionist procurement policies.
“There is a gap between the threats of today and an armed force that will only be ready in a few years,” Eichelsheim stated during the summit, which also featured addresses from NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte and top European Union security officials. He emphasized that during this transitional phase, maintaining robust deterrence is paramount, and if deterrence fails, European forces must be prepared to fight.
The 'Tinder' Analogy for Defense Procurement
In a striking critique of current European defense collaboration mechanisms, the Dutch general compared the bloc's matchmaking tools for defense projects to the dating application Tinder.
Eichelsheim argued that existing European Union frameworks designed to connect member states with defense industry projects suffer from the same frustrations as modern dating apps. “Right now, it is like Tinder, with all the associated frustrations,” he told the audience of defense contractors and policymakers.
“To find a match, you need enough participants on the platform, and once a match appears, someone has to act. It is clear that member states, including my own, do not register all their projects on this platform.”
He further noted that the profiles submitted by nations and contractors often lack the necessary detail to facilitate meaningful partnerships, much like incomplete dating profiles. Even when a theoretical match is made, the follow-through from national capitals is frequently absent.
Fragmented Programs and National Interests
The core of Eichelsheim's argument centered on the inefficiency of prioritizing domestic industrial returns over collective military capability. He pointed to the proliferation of redundant systems across the bloc, noting that Europe does not need 27 different drone programs to achieve its security objectives.
“Too often, we start by asking: 'What share of the defense industry contracts can my own country get?' Only after we establish that do we look at partners and accept attempts to make defense cooperation work,” he explained. “We must reverse this logic.”
The general stressed that success should not be measured by the volume of joint programs launched, but by tangible equipment delivered to soldiers. This shift requires member states to pool resources and accept that not every nation will secure a primary manufacturing role.
Strategic Implications for NATO and the EU
The warnings from the Dutch defense chief arrive at a critical juncture for transatlantic security. With ongoing debates regarding the future of United States commitments to European defense and the persistent threat of Russian hybrid and conventional aggression, the pressure on European capitals to achieve strategic autonomy has intensified.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, also present at the summit, echoed the need for heightened readiness. He noted that while there may be no immediate threat to NATO territory, the alliance must prepare for a protracted era of strategic competition.
For the European Union, the challenge lies in translating increased defense budgets into interoperable, scalable forces. Initiatives like the European Defence Fund and the Permanent Structured Cooperation (PESCO) have generated numerous projects, but critics argue they remain too fragmented to deliver rapid, large-scale capability enhancements.
Eichelsheim's intervention underscores a growing consensus among senior European military leaders: without a fundamental restructuring of how the continent buys and builds military hardware, the promised rearmament of Europe will remain a bureaucratic exercise rather than a operational reality. The window to close the vulnerability gap before 2030, he cautioned, is narrowing rapidly.
Industrial Base Constraints and Drone Proliferation
The general's specific reference to “27 different drone programs” highlights a chronic issue within the European defense industrial base. Unlike the United States, which benefits from a consolidated market and massive economies of scale, Europe's defense sector is fractured along national lines. This fragmentation drives up unit costs, complicates logistics, and hinders interoperability during joint multinational operations.
Efforts to consolidate the market have historically been blocked by member states eager to protect domestic champions and preserve high-skilled manufacturing jobs. However, the modern battlefield, characterized by the mass deployment of uncrewed aerial systems, demands rapid iteration and standardized production runs that the current fragmented model struggles to support.
| European Defense Cooperation Challenges |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Challenge Area | Current Reality | Required Shift | 
|---|---|---|
| Procurement Logic | Prioritizes national industrial return (juste retour) | Prioritizes rapid capability delivery to forces | 
| System Standardization | Multiple redundant platforms (e.g., 27 drone programs) | Consolidated, interoperable systems across NATO/EU | 
| Project Matching | Fragmented data, low participation in EU portals | Transparent, mandatory reporting of capability needs | 
By reversing the procurement logic, Eichelsheim argues that Europe could leverage its combined economic weight to secure better technology and faster delivery times. The alternative, he suggests, is a continued reliance on off-the-shelf purchases from external allies or a prolonged period where European forces operate with suboptimal, disjointed equipment.
